Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

WASHINGTON (CNN) -- The White House is blasting Congressional Democrats for not sending a bill that would fund veterans' care programs to the president's desk by Veterans Day. The White House's Dana Perino accused Democrats of holding veterans care funding hostage. "There's absolutely no reason that the veterans' bill could not have been signed by the president today, except for the political games that the Democrats decided to play with it," White House press secretary Dana Perino said Sunday in Crawford, Texas. Congressional Democrats had attached legislation funding veterans programs to a $150.7 billion bill that also funded a number of domestic priorities, including health, labor and education. Democrats also added $3.7 billion to what the president budgeted for veterans programs. The labor-health-education bill would increase funding by more than $10 billion over last year's funding for those programs. The president has threatened to veto the bill because of the added spending. The House passed a health-labor-education bill 269-142 last week with the veterans funding attached, but the Senate later voted to strip out the veterans funding and send the health-labor-education bill to the president. Perino accused the Democrats of "trying to hold hostage our veterans to extra domestic spending or increases in taxes." "The president wants clean legislation, a clean bill to fund the veterans," Perino said. On Saturday, the Democratic congressional leadership sent a letter to President Bush saying they welcomed a dialogue on spending, sayings disagreements over funding levels "have never been so great that we cannot reach agreement on a spending plan that meets the needs of the American people." "Key to this dialogue, however, is some willingness on your part to actually find common ground," House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-California, and Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, D-Nevada, said in the letter. The leadership said last year's Congress, which was still under Republican control, had never passed a separate bill funding veterans programs. Congress also sent to the president legislation that would fund veterans care at the levels requested by the president through December 14, the leadership said. The current funding level "is still below the $3.9 billion extra that we passed," said Nadeam Elshami, spokesman Pelosi. "We are committed to getting the extra funding that the Congress already voted on the president's desk for his signature." The leadership blamed Republican members of Congress for stalling the funding for the veterans programs by blocking its inclusion in the larger spending bill. Perino, though, said the Democrats could still send a separate bill to the president funding the veterans program that passed both chambers of Congress. "The Democrats decided not to send the president this bill," Perino said. "That has to be laid at their feet." E-mail to a friend . CNN's Deirdre Walsh contributed to this report.

WASHINGTON (CNN) — The White House is criticizing congressional Democrats for failing to send a bill funding veterans’ care programs to the president’s desk by Veterans Day.

White House press secretary Dana Perino accused Democrats of holding veterans’ care funding hostage.

“There’s absolutely no reason that the veterans’ bill could not have been signed by the president today, except for the political games that the Democrats decided to play with it,” Perino said Sunday in Crawford, Texas.

Congressional Democrats had attached legislation funding veterans’ programs to a $150.7 billion bill that also funded a number of domestic priorities, including health, labor, and education. Democrats also added $3.7 billion to the amount the president had budgeted for veterans’ programs.

The labor-health-education bill would increase funding for those programs by more than $10 billion over last year’s levels. The president has threatened to veto the measure because of the additional spending.

The House passed a health-labor-education bill last week, 269-142, with the veterans’ funding attached. The Senate later voted to remove the veterans’ funding and send the health-labor-education bill to the president.

Perino accused Democrats of “trying to hold hostage our veterans to extra domestic spending or increases in taxes.”

“The president wants clean legislation, a clean bill to fund the veterans,” Perino said.

On Saturday, Democratic congressional leaders sent a letter to President Bush saying they welcomed a dialogue on spending, noting that disagreements over funding levels “have never been so great that we cannot reach agreement on a spending plan that meets the needs of the American people.”

“Key to this dialogue, however, is some willingness on your part to actually find common ground,” House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-California, and Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, D-Nevada, said in the letter.

The leadership said last year’s Congress, which was still under Republican control, had not passed a separate bill funding veterans’ programs. Congress also sent the president legislation that would fund veterans’ care at the levels requested by the president through December 14, the leadership said.

The current funding level “is still below the $3.9 billion extra that we passed,” said Nadeam Elshami, spokesman for Pelosi. “We are committed to getting the extra funding that the Congress already voted on to the president’s desk for his signature.”

The leadership blamed Republican members of Congress for delaying funding for veterans’ programs by blocking its inclusion in the larger spending bill.

Perino, however, said Democrats could still send the president a separate bill funding the veterans’ program that had passed both chambers of Congress.

“The Democrats decided not to send the president this bill,” Perino said. “That has to be laid at their feet.”

CNN’s Deirdre Walsh contributed to this report.

WASHINGTON (CNN) — The White House criticized Democratic leaders in Congress for failing to deliver legislation funding veterans’ care programs to President Bush in time for Veterans Day.

White House press secretary Dana Perino accused Democrats of using veterans’ health funding as leverage. Speaking Sunday in Crawford, Texas, Perino said there was “absolutely no reason” the president could not have signed the veterans bill that day, other than what she described as political maneuvering by Democrats.

Democrats in Congress had combined veterans program funding with a $150.7 billion spending measure that also covered several domestic priorities, among them health, labor and education programs. They also included $3.7 billion more for veterans programs than the amount requested in the president’s budget. Overall, the labor-health-education measure would raise funding for those programs by more than $10 billion compared with the previous year.

President Bush has said he would veto the bill because of the additional spending.

The House approved the health-labor-education package last week by a vote of 269-142, with the veterans funding included. The Senate later voted to remove the veterans funding and forward the health-labor-education bill to the president separately.

Perino said Democrats were attempting to “hold hostage” veterans in order to secure higher domestic spending or tax increases. She said the president wanted a separate, straightforward measure devoted only to veterans funding.

On Saturday, Democratic congressional leaders sent Bush a letter saying they were open to discussing spending issues. They wrote that disagreements over funding amounts “have never been so great” that an agreement could not be reached on a plan serving the needs of Americans.

House Speaker Nancy Pelosi of California and Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid of Nevada said in the letter that meaningful talks would require Bush to show a willingness to seek compromise.

Democratic leaders also noted that the previous Congress, then controlled by Republicans, had not passed a stand-alone bill to fund veterans programs. They said Congress had already sent the president legislation that would finance veterans care at the levels he requested through December 14.

Nadeam Elshami, a spokesman for Pelosi, said that current funding remains below the additional $3.9 billion approved by Congress. He said Democrats were committed to sending the extra veterans funding already passed by Congress to the president for his signature.

Democratic leaders blamed Republican lawmakers for delaying veterans program funding by preventing it from being included in the broader spending measure.

Perino rejected that argument, saying Democrats still had the option of sending Bush a separate veterans funding bill that had already cleared both the House and Senate. She said the responsibility rested with Democrats because they chose not to send the president that legislation.

CNN’s Deirdre Walsh contributed to this report.

**White House accuses Democrats of delaying veterans care funding by tying it to broader spending package**

**Washington** — The White House is criticizing congressional Democrats for what it says is an unnecessary delay in approving funding for veterans’ health care, accusing lawmakers of attaching the measure to a larger domestic spending bill as Veterans Day approaches.

Administration officials argue that money for veterans’ medical services should move through Congress on its own, rather than be wrapped into a broader package that includes other domestic priorities. The White House says the delay risks turning a traditionally bipartisan issue into another flashpoint in the ongoing fight over federal spending.

“Veterans’ care should never be used as leverage in a broader political negotiation,” a White House official said, calling on Congress to pass the funding separately and quickly.

Democratic lawmakers, however, have defended the broader spending bill, saying it reflects a range of urgent national needs and includes critical investments in health care, housing, education and community programs alongside funding for veterans. They argue that Republicans and the White House are attempting to isolate one politically sensitive portion of the bill while opposing other domestic programs.

The dispute comes at a sensitive time on Capitol Hill, with lawmakers facing pressure to act before Veterans Day, when elected officials from both parties typically emphasize their support for former service members. Veterans groups have long warned against disruptions in funding for Department of Veterans Affairs programs, particularly amid rising demand for health care, mental health services and benefits processing.

The White House’s criticism is part of a broader messaging push over federal spending, as both parties seek to blame the other for delays in appropriations. Republicans have frequently accused Democrats of using must-pass funding measures to advance unrelated priorities, while Democrats counter that GOP opposition to broader domestic spending threatens programs that millions of Americans rely on.

It remains unclear whether congressional leaders will agree to separate the veterans funding from the larger package. Negotiations are expected to continue in the coming days, with lawmakers weighing both the political optics and the practical consequences of delaying funds for veterans’ services.

For now, the fight has placed veterans funding at the center of a familiar Washington standoff — one unfolding just as the country prepares to honor those who served.

**Bush White House, Democrats clash over veterans funding and domestic spending bill**

**WASHINGTON (CNN)** — The Bush administration and Democratic congressional leaders are locked in a dispute over veterans funding, with the White House accusing Democrats of tying needed veterans’ programs to a broader domestic spending bill that President George W. Bush has threatened to veto.

At the center of the fight is a large labor, health and education appropriations bill that includes funding for programs such as education, job training, medical research and health services. Democrats have also linked veterans-related funding to the broader spending package, arguing that both veterans’ care and domestic priorities deserve increased support.

The White House says the measure spends too much and exceeds the president’s budget limits. Administration officials have called on Congress to send Bush a “clean” veterans bill — legislation focused solely on veterans’ programs — rather than attaching veterans funding to a larger bill the president opposes.

Democratic leaders counter that the administration is trying to avoid responsibility for opposing increases in domestic programs while using veterans as a political shield. They argue that their spending plan reflects national priorities, including better health care and services for veterans returning from Iraq and Afghanistan.

The dispute reflects a broader budget standoff between Bush and the Democratic-controlled Congress. Democrats have pushed for billions of dollars more than the president requested in domestic spending, saying the money is needed for education, health care, labor programs and veterans’ services. Bush has repeatedly vowed to veto bills that exceed his spending targets, saying Democrats are being fiscally irresponsible.

Republicans have framed the issue as a test of whether Democrats will separate veterans funding from the larger labor-health-education bill. Democrats, meanwhile, say the president is threatening to block popular programs while demanding Congress follow his budget priorities.

The fight has intensified because veterans’ programs typically enjoy strong bipartisan support, making them politically difficult to oppose. Both sides say they support veterans, but each accuses the other of using veterans’ funding as leverage in a larger spending battle.

If Congress sends the broader bill to the White House and Bush vetoes it, lawmakers would have to decide whether to rewrite the legislation, attempt to override the veto, or pass a narrower veterans measure separately.

**Bush White House criticizes Congress over veterans funding bill on Veterans Day**

**WASHINGTON** — The White House marked Veterans Day by criticizing Congress for failing to send President George W. Bush a veterans care funding bill, escalating a dispute with Democratic leaders over spending priorities and responsibility for delays in funding government programs.

White House press secretary Dana Perino said the president was disappointed that lawmakers had not completed work on legislation funding veterans medical care and other military-related programs before the holiday honoring those who served in the armed forces.

“Congress has had months to get this work done,” Perino said, arguing that veterans “should not have to wait” while lawmakers debate broader spending bills.

The dispute centers on a military construction and veterans affairs appropriations bill, one of several annual spending measures Congress had not completed. The Bush administration has repeatedly accused the Democratic-controlled Congress of moving too slowly on appropriations and of seeking spending levels above the president’s budget request.

Democratic leaders rejected the criticism, saying they had pushed for increased funding for veterans care after years of war in Iraq and Afghanistan. They argued that the administration was trying to shift blame despite opposing Democratic spending plans.

House Speaker Nancy Pelosi and Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid have said Democrats are committed to improving veterans services, including treatment for wounded troops returning from combat.

“Democrats have made veterans’ health care a top priority,” Democratic leaders said, accusing the White House of resisting needed increases in funding.

The Veterans Day clash came amid a broader battle between Bush and congressional Democrats over domestic spending and war policy. The president has threatened vetoes of several spending bills, saying they exceed his budget limits. Democrats counter that the administration’s fiscal objections are misplaced given the cost of the wars overseas.

Veterans groups have long pressed both parties to increase funding for medical care, disability claims processing and services for troops returning from Iraq and Afghanistan, including treatment for traumatic brain injury and post-traumatic stress disorder.

The White House said Bush remained committed to supporting service members and veterans, pointing to funding increases during his administration. Democrats said the unfinished legislation reflected Republican resistance and presidential veto threats, not a lack of concern from Congress.

The standoff left the veterans funding measure caught in a larger appropriations fight, with both sides using Veterans Day to argue they were the stronger advocate for those who served.

**WASHINGTON (CNN-style report) —** A fight over veterans’ health care and domestic spending escalated in Washington in 2007 as congressional Democrats accused President George W. Bush of threatening needed increases for veterans, education and health programs, while the White House charged that Democratic leaders were using veterans as political cover for a broader spending increase.

At issue was the fiscal 2008 budget and a series of annual appropriations bills moving through the Democratic-controlled Congress. House Speaker Nancy Pelosi and Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid argued that their budget plan made overdue investments in domestic priorities after years of war-related spending and tight limits on non-defense programs under the Bush administration.

The White House countered that Democrats were seeking roughly **$22 billion more** in domestic discretionary spending than the president had requested and warned that Bush would veto appropriations bills that exceeded his limits.

The sharpest rhetoric centered on funding for the Department of Veterans Affairs, particularly veterans’ medical care, at a time when the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan had put new demands on the VA system. Democrats promoted their budget as a major increase for veterans’ health services, saying the money was necessary to treat wounded service members and aging veterans and to address problems highlighted by reports of inadequate care for some returning troops.

Pelosi and Reid said the administration was preparing to block those increases as part of a broader effort to hold down domestic spending.

“The president’s veto threats would deny critical funding for veterans’ health care,” Democrats argued in substance, portraying the fight as a test of national priorities: whether the government would provide for troops after they returned home as well as fund the wars abroad.

White House press secretary **Dana Perino** rejected that framing, saying Bush supported veterans but would not accept what the administration viewed as excessive spending by Congress. Perino accused Democrats of trying to “hide” or “mask” billions in additional domestic spending behind popular programs such as veterans care.

The administration’s position was that veterans’ funding should move forward, but not as part of a package that exceeded the president’s overall spending targets. Perino said Democrats were attempting to portray Bush as opposing veterans when, in the White House’s view, the dispute was really over the size of the federal budget.

The clash reflected a broader political struggle after Democrats won control of Congress in the 2006 midterm elections. With Bush weakened politically and the Iraq war deeply unpopular, Pelosi and Reid sought to use the budget process to shift money toward domestic programs and oversight priorities. The White House, meanwhile, tried to reassert fiscal discipline by drawing a line against what it called runaway spending.

Democrats emphasized that their proposed increases included money for veterans’ medical services, military health care, education, medical research, law enforcement, and other domestic needs. They said the additional spending was modest compared with the cost of the Iraq war and tax cuts enacted earlier in Bush’s presidency.

Republicans and White House officials argued that the Democratic plan would put the country on a path toward higher taxes and larger deficits. They said Congress should meet the president’s spending cap and send him clean appropriations bills rather than force confrontations over politically sensitive programs.

The fight also came amid intense scrutiny of veterans’ care following revelations earlier in 2007 about poor conditions and bureaucratic failures at Walter Reed Army Medical Center, which treated wounded troops. Although Walter Reed was run by the Army rather than the VA, the scandal intensified pressure on both parties to demonstrate commitment to military personnel and veterans.

For Democrats, veterans funding became a central argument in their case that the Bush budget failed to meet real needs. For the White House, the issue became an example of what it said was Democratic budget politics: attaching popular spending increases to broader bills and daring the president to veto them.

The standoff foreshadowed a series of veto threats and negotiations over appropriations bills throughout 2007. Bush had already shown a willingness to use his veto pen more aggressively after Democrats took control of Capitol Hill, including in disputes over Iraq war policy and domestic spending.

In the budget fight, both sides claimed the mantle of fiscal responsibility and support for veterans. Democrats said they were correcting years of underfunding. The White House said it was willing to fund veterans but not to approve an overall spending level it considered excessive.

The dispute underscored the political power of veterans’ issues in wartime Washington — and the difficulty of separating funding for widely supported programs from the larger battle over taxes, deficits and the role of government.
